name: a-crosshatch-wide-autumn
prompt: A hand-drawn pen-and-ink newspaper cartoon from around 1919, black ink only on warm off-white newsprint, built entirely from fine nib lines: tone made by dense crosshatching that thickens into near-solid black in the shadows and thins to sparse parallel strokes in the light, line weight swelling and tapering with pen pressure, slight ink spread at the edges, no grey wash and no colour. Tall vertical frame. Eye level with the seat, camera dead square to a slatted wrought-iron park bench, both figures shown head to boot. The bench stands beneath a leafless plane tree whose mottled trunk rises at the left edge; curled fallen leaves lie scattered on the gravel path and a few drift in the air. A grossly fat rich man in a tall silk hat occupies two-thirds of the bench, legs spread wide, his checked waistcoat strained to bursting across a huge round belly, a watch chain looped over it, spats on his shoes; his head is turned away in bored disdain and one gloved hand flicks outward, brushing the other man off like a crumb. Wedged onto the remaining third sits a gaunt young soldier in a shabby army greatcoat, cap in his lap, one trouser leg empty and folded up with a safety pin, a wooden crutch leaning on the bench arm beside him; he looks up at the rich man with quiet, tired patience. Flat, even daylight with shadows falling to the right beneath the bench. The upper quarter of the image is left as plain, almost untouched pale sky, only a faint scratch of hatching at its lower edge, as open space above the scene. No words, letters, captions, signatures or speech balloons anywhere in the picture. Thanks.

name: a-grease-crayon-low-angle
prompt: Editorial drawing made with a blunt stick of black lithographic grease crayon dragged across coarse, toothy off-white newsprint, over a faint watery grey ink wash, in the rough protest-magazine manner of 1919 rather than neat pen hatching. We look up from ground level on a gravel park path, the eye just above the stones, at a slatted bench in a bare post-war city park. Filling the upper two thirds sits a huge, overfed plutocrat: stovepipe hat, heavy astrakhan-collared greatcoat buttoned tight over his paunch, gold fob glinting across the waistcoat, spats and polished boots planted near the lens so the foreshortening makes him rise like a bronze monument on a plinth against a low, sullen, colourless sky. He thrusts one flat, fleshy palm sideways in a brusque halt, a lit cigar pinched in the other fist, eyelids drooping with boredom. Tucked into the lower right corner, drawn small, a gaunt young demobbed private in a shabby khaki tunic and peaked cap, his left leg ending at the knee with the empty fabric folded and pinned, a plain timber crutch resting over his thighs, half his face swallowed by crayon shadow. Every tone is built from the crayon alone: thick sideways strokes, crumbling soft edges where the wax skipped the paper grain, solid blacks massed in the coat and hat, sparse flecked texture in the clouds. Only black, smoky grey wash and the warm off-white of the sheet. The lowest fifth of the frame is bare pale gravel with nothing in it, left open for a caption. No words, letters, signature or speech balloons appear on the page. Thanks.

name: a-two-colour-overhead
prompt: Tall upright weekly-magazine plate from 1919, pulled on a letterpress in only two inks on warm cream stock: a black key drawing, with one flat brick-red (#A63A2B) laid over it as a separate plate and nudged a hair out of register. The viewpoint perches at the crown of an iron lamp standard and stares almost straight down at a park bench in deep winter. Bench, raked gravel walk and the stretched shadows of leafless plane trees all run together in one hard slant from bottom left to top right, splitting the page in two. At the bench's left end, foreshortened from above, sits an enormous round plutocrat: the glossy black disc of his topper, sloping coat shoulders, a starched wing collar, and bulging between his lapels a waistcoat that holds the only red anywhere on the plate, its flat red sprinkled with rows of minute dollar signs. One gloved arm swings outward, away from his neighbour, palm flicking the air the way you would shoo off a waiter. At the far end, empty slats gaping between them, a gaunt demobbed private hunches in a shabby army greatcoat and field cap; his left leg stops at the knee, the empty khaki pinned up flat, his right foot in a hobnailed boot planted on the gravel, a rough ash-wood crutch leaning beside him. Low winter sun stretches the crutch and that lone boot into two long, thin black shadows that stripe across the walk by themselves. Brisk dip-pen line, ruled parallel hatching in the shade, solid black on hat and coats; the red has no outline of its own; faint ink spread and visible paper tooth. The top fifth of the sheet stays bare cream paper, nothing drawn there at all. No lettering, words, monograms or speech balloons anywhere on the plate. Thanks.

name: b-crosshatch-hospital-dusk
prompt: Tall upright drawing in the manner of an early twentieth-century newspaper cartoon, built entirely from black ink lines laid down with a dip pen on off-white newsprint: shadow made only by stacked layers of crisscrossed strokes, confident thick outlines, no washes, no grey tones, no colour at all. The view sits at seated head height, square on to a wooden-slatted public bench with curled cast-iron ends, which fills the lower half of the picture. On the bench's left end lounges a portly tycoon exactly as he was a century ago and unchanged by it: tall silk top hat, frock coat, a buttoned waistcoat stretched over a round belly with a watch chain, striped trousers, white spats over polished shoes, legs crossed, chin lifted, eyes half-closed in boredom, one gloved hand tossed outward in a lazy brush-off toward his neighbour. On the right end slumps a young nurse of today in loose hospital scrubs, a lanyard with a plastic ID card hanging at her chest, chunky running trainers, a takeaway coffee cup held in both hands on her knees, eyes closed, head tipped back against the slats, utterly spent. The surroundings are present-day yet drawn with the same old-fashioned nib: a wheelie-style park rubbish bin beside the bench, a slim modern street lamp with a phone-charging socket on its post, bare winter trees, and beyond their branches a large hospital tower inked into near-total darkness, its lighted windows left as neat grids of small untouched white oblongs. Evening is falling, the last light glowing low behind the tower, the hatching thickening toward the paths and the ground. Above all this, the top fourth of the page is left as bare, almost unmarked paper sky with only a few wisps of line, an open band where words will later be set. Pure line art; no lettering, no speech balloons, no signature.

name: b-crayon-closeup-hands
prompt: Vertical waist-up close shot of two people sharing a wooden park bench, rendered as an old newspaper opinion-page drawing: broad, broken strokes of black lithographic grease crayon scrubbed over coarse off-white paper so the tooth shows through, with puddled washes of thinned India ink and a few scratched-out white highlights. Nearest to us, square in the middle, a fleshy hand in a pale kid glove is lifted palm outward in a lazy brush-off gesture; it is drawn hard and exact, every knuckle crease outlined in firm dark line, the crispest mark on the page. Just past that hand, rendered in gentler, half-dissolved crayon with rubbed edges, a worn-out present-day nurse in creased scrubs leans toward him, lips parted mid-word, fingers spread flat on her breastbone, a plastic hospital pass on a lanyard at her chest, eyebrows pulled together. He sits to the right: a heavy, well-fed gentleman with a high black top hat, starched wing collar and a watch chain stretched across a bulging waistcoat, nose lifted, lids lowered, gazing straight ahead as though she were not there. A low raking light comes from the left, leaving her cheekbone and his raised glove as bare paper, while everything toward the right edge drowns in thick, waxy, glossy crayon black that eats into his frock coat. Across the lowest strip of the composition runs a trimmed hedge, a dark mass of quick zigzag crayon scribble with nothing in front of it, kept clear for words to be added later. Monochrome only: crayon black, ink greys and the warm white of the paper. Leave out all lettering, balloons, labels and signatures. Thanks.

name: b-laid-paper-rain
prompt: Upright newspaper-cartoon drawing made only with a black dip pen on heavy cream laid paper whose ribbing stays visible across the whole sheet: wide-spaced chain lines running top to bottom and close fine laid lines crossing them, the ink catching on the raised ribs and skipping the hollows, so every mid-tone comes from that broken striped grain plus hundreds of thin parallel rain strokes all slanting the same way down to the right, irregularly spaced, some dashed and overlapping, with no brush wash and no flat grey areas. The present day, a medium-wide view from seated height of an ordinary slatted park bench on shining wet tarmac. On the left sits a portly, double-chinned plutocrat wearing a high black stovepipe hat, a buttoned frock coat straining over his paunch and a gold fob dangling at his belly, bone dry under a huge black umbrella tilted to shelter him and nobody else, one gloved hand flapping lazily toward the woman beside him to wave her away, lids drooping, nose in the air. On the right, beyond the dripping rim of his umbrella, a worn-out nurse in hospital scrubs and a thin knitted cardigan sits soaked and hunched, wet hair stuck to her cheeks, a cloth tote bag clutched on her knees, eyes on him. Behind the bench, rain rings spread across puddles that reflect the bench legs, and a modern bus shelter of glass panels and steel posts is sketched in sparse fine outline. Dull overcast daylight with no shadows to speak of; the umbrella canopy is the only solid black mass. Black ink on cream paper and nothing more. Across the top third the drawing simply stops: bare ribbed sheet, grazed by a few faint falling streaks, left empty so words can be set over it afterwards. No lettering, no words on the shelter, no signature on the sheet. Thanks.

name: c-split-diptych
prompt: A tall portrait sheet of illustration board inked by hand in the manner of a front-page newspaper drawing from the year the Great War ended: black india ink laid over light graphite, lines that swell where the nib pressed and taper to hairs at their tips, tone built from crossing diagonal strokes that pack into solid black under the bench and inside the hat, and a faint ribbed texture of laid paper showing through the pale areas. A single thin inked rule, slightly wobbly as if pulled freehand along a ruler, divides the board into two stacked scenes of equal height, and between them lies a clean horizontal band of bare white board about a fifth of the sheet tall, nothing drawn in it. In the top scene, a gravel walk in a city park just after the armistice: bare elms, a gas lamp, a wrought-iron bench with slatted seat, seen straight on from a crouching height. On the bench's left end lounges a heavy, prosperous gentleman: jowls spilling over a winged collar, small clipped moustache, tall glossy silk topper, frock coat strained across a round belly, gold chain across the waistcoat, cane propped between his spats, his free hand lifted beside his ear with the palm turned out, brushing someone away, eyes half shut, chin tipped up. On the right end sits a gaunt young doughboy in a wrinkled khaki tunic, a single boot on the gravel and the other trouser leg pinned up short and empty below the thigh, a wooden crutch across his lap, overseas cap crumpled in his fist, leaning toward the gentleman as if to ask something. In the bottom scene, the very same bench from the very same spot, but the park is now: a steel litter bin, an LED lamp post, a parked hire bicycle, a glass office block rising behind the trees, all hatched in the identical ink. The gentleman is reproduced line for line, the same size, at the same place on the bench, the same lifted brushing hand, the same half-shut eyes and tipped chin, the same shine on the topper, so that his two figures stack one directly over the other like two pulls from one engraving. Beside him now slumps a worn-out night-shift nurse in loose scrubs and trainers, a lanyard at her neck, a paper cup going cold in her lap, turning toward him with the same hopeful lean the soldier had. Everything around him has changed; he has not changed by one line. Even, diffuse daylight with no cast shadows, pure black ink on off-white board, no colour, no grey wash. No writing anywhere in the picture: no words, letters, numbers, signature or speech balloons.

name: c-portrait-straight-to-camera
prompt: A tall upright sheet of warm ivory paper carrying one figure drawn in black ink with a fine pen: a stout, well-fed gentleman of about 1919, invented for this picture and resembling no real person, seated squarely at the centre of a plain slatted park bench and facing us dead on, the eye level of the drawing at his chest so we see him whole from polished spats to the crown of a tall glossy silk hat. He leans back at ease, thighs spread to make room for a round belly buttoned into a tight double-breasted waistcoat with a watch chain looped across it, a long dark tailcoat open at the front, a cane propped against one knee with his gloved hand folded over its knob. Fleshy chins, neat waxed moustache, small hooded eyes fixed on ours, mouth turned up at one corner in a quiet, contented smile, as if he has just been proved right again. The seat on his right is bare except for a wooden crutch fallen flat across the slats; the seat on his left is bare except for a modern hospital pass on its cord, slipped half over the edge, its card blank. No park around him: no trees, lamps or path, just the empty paper, one short horizontal stroke for the ground and a little hatched shadow pooled under the bench. Flat, shadowless, frontal light like a costume study, so every button and fold reads plainly. All shading is built from line alone: dense cross-hatching in the coat and hat, finer single-direction strokes on the trousers, a few dots of stipple on the cheeks, the face kept mostly open. Ink black on ivory only, no colour, no wash, no grey tones. The upper third of the sheet, above the hat, is left as clean empty paper with nothing drawn in it; no words, letters, numbers, signature or speech balloon on the sheet at all. Thanks.

name: c-red-spot-repeated-benches
prompt: Tall portrait drawing in rough black grease crayon and quick pen strokes on cream newsprint with a toothy grain, printed in black plus one flat spot of red, like an old two-ink newspaper page. A straight gravel walk recedes from our feet in one-point perspective toward a vanishing point slightly above centre, lined with leafless elms and an endless row of matching wooden slatted benches that diminish until they vanish into a speck. Every bench holds the same stout rich man, duplicated without variation: tall black stovepipe hat, heavy jowls, cigar, legs crossed identically, one gloved hand raised in a lazy flick of dismissal, his straining waistcoat filled with solid red and marked with a black dollar sign. Red appears nowhere else, so those waistcoats make a dotted trail that pulls the eye down the walk. Beside him the companion differs on each bench: closest and largest, filling the lower foreground, a worn-out nurse in baggy scrubs with hands folded on her knees; next a coal miner with a sooty face and a cap lamp; then a factory girl in a long apron and headscarf; far down, just a few marks, a soldier on a crutch whose empty left leg is pinned up. Camera at seated eye level on the gravel, as if we are next to sit down. Flat even daylight, scratchy crayon shadow beneath each bench, dense black hatching on the tree trunks, bare paper left white for highlights. The upper third is blank pale sky with faint crayon tooth, open space for words to be laid over later; the drawing itself carries no writing, letters or signature. Thanks.
